# How the proof works: Kourovka 21.3, first question

**Agent-generated exposition; not refereed.** This informal account was generated by **Nilradical v0** after [human acceptance](../nilradical-v0-acceptance/README.md) of the linked proof snapshot. It has not been refereed and may simplify details. The exact mathematical claims are the linked Lean statements and proofs; acceptance of that snapshot does not imply human review of this prose.

## The question and the uniform cutoff

The answer is affirmative in every sufficiently large degree: any two soluble subgroups of $S_n$ have a conjugate with trivial intersection, and the same holds inside $A_n$ with an even conjugator. The problem, posed by M. Anagnostopoulou-Merkouri and T. C. Burness, also asks whether degree 21 already suffices. That explicit threshold is outside this result. Nilradical v0 supplies the solution and Lean proof of the first question, as recorded in the [accepted problem overview](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/README.md).

The quantifiers matter. [`FirstQuestion`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Statement.lean#L23) asks for one natural number $N$ before choosing either the degree $n \ge N$ or the subgroups $H$ and $K$. For the alternating case, the subgroups are represented as subgroups of $S_n$ with explicit containment in $A_n$. The conclusion explicitly requires $x \in A_n$. Lean's subgroup relation `Disjoint` means that the intersection is the trivial subgroup, and `MulAut.conj x⁻¹ • K` denotes $x^{-1}Kx$. Thus no change of conjugation convention or subgroup model weakens the question.

The proof obtains more information than existence in the symmetric group. For each pair $H$, $K$, let its success probability be the proportion of all $x \in S_n$ satisfying $H \cap x^{-1}Kx = 1$. Let $p_n$ be the infimum of these probabilities over all soluble pairs in that degree. The theorem [`asymptoticStatement`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/Asymptotic.lean#L17) proves

$$
p_n \longrightarrow \exp\!\left(-\frac{9}{2}\right).
$$

Since this limit is positive, eventually every pair has at least one successful conjugator. The use of an infimum across all pairs is what makes the cutoff uniform.

This probability model is entirely finite. [`successProbability`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/Basic.lean#L57) is a cardinality divided by $|S_n|$, interpreted in the real numbers. [`worstProbability`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/Basic.lean#L102) is the corresponding infimum. The set being minimized is nonempty, since the trivial subgroup is soluble, and all its values lie between zero and one. The formal proof therefore connects its analytic limit to actual permutations, rather than to a surrogate random variable.

## The transposition core and the limiting probability

The main structural device isolates the transpositions. The [`transpositionCore`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/TranspositionCore.lean#L25) of $H$ is generated by all transpositions contained in $H$. A group generated by transpositions contains every permutation within each of its orbits: connected chains of swaps generate the full symmetric group there. Consequently a soluble $H$ cannot have a core orbit with five or more points, since it would contain a nonsoluble symmetric group. This is proved by [`ncard_transpositionCore_orbit_le_four`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/TranspositionCore.lean#L125).

The two cores can therefore be described by partitions into blocks of size at most four. After randomly relabelling one partition, the cores intersect trivially exactly when no two points lie together in a block of both partitions. Such a pair is called a collision. If $a$ and $b$ count the unordered within-block pairs in the two partitions, the expected number of collisions is $2ab/(n(n-1))$. Each point has at most three partners, so $a$ and $b$ are at most $3n/2$. The mean is consequently at most $\frac{9}{2}\frac{n}{n-1}$, explaining the constant $9/2$. The exact mean is formalized in [`collisionMean_eq`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/YoungConfigurationCount.lean#L313).

The mean alone does not give the required probability of zero collisions. The combinatorial argument counts families of collision witnesses and controls their overlaps. For every fixed order, the normalized binomial moments approach the corresponding Poisson expression, uniformly over all allowed partitions. Finite Bonferroni inequalities then bound the zero-collision probability. A controlled exponential-series remainder turns those finitely many moment estimates into an eventual lower bound $\exp(-9/2) - \varepsilon$. The analytic bridge is [`uniformConfigurationLowerAsymptotic_of_moments`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/UniformBrunLower.lean#L130). Uniformity is essential again: partitions may change with $n$ and with the chosen groups.

## Controlling the remaining group elements

Trivial intersection of the cores does not yet exclude an element common to the original groups. To control that error, the proof embeds each soluble permutation action in a soluble envelope built recursively using direct products and wreath products. A forest records this recursive action. Encodings of elements by their moved points and their positions in the forest give uniform support counts, with a stronger estimate for elements outside the core. Conjugation counting converts these estimates into an error bounded by a fixed summable majorant divided by $n$. It therefore tends to zero. [`positiveSupportEnvelopeBounds`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/ForestEnvelopeBounds.lean#L124) supplies these bounds without a classification premise. Enlarging $H$ and $K$ only makes successful conjugation harder, so the envelope estimates imply the desired lower bound for the original groups.

A matching upper bound shows that the limiting constant is sharp for this worst-case probability. Partition the points into consecutive blocks of four, with a final smaller block if necessary, and take the product of the symmetric groups on those blocks. This group is soluble, and it already equals its transposition core. Each full block contributes six unordered pairs, making the pair density approach $3/2$. The collision mean approaches $9/2$, and the moment calculation gives success probability tending to $\exp(-9/2)$. The result is [`tendsto_fourBlockSuccessProbability`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/UpperWitness.lean#L651). Squeezing $p_n$ between the uniform lower estimate and this explicit family's probabilities proves the limit.

## Obtaining an even conjugator

The alternating argument needs a further step: positivity among all permutations does not automatically yield an even witness. Enlarge the two given groups to maximal soluble subgroups. If either overgroup contains an odd permutation, multiplication on the appropriate side changes the parity of a good conjugator while preserving its goodness for those overgroups. If both overgroups lie in $A_n$, they contain no transpositions and their cores are trivial. Maximality identifies them with their soluble envelopes, so the noncore estimate applies directly. Eventually fewer than $|S_n|/2$ permutations are bad, whereas exactly $|S_n|/2$ are even. Some even permutation must therefore be good.

The proof combines the two eventual conclusions in [`eventually_kourovka213`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Proof/AlternatingAsymptotic.lean#L157). The short public theorem [`Kourovka.P21_03.firstQuestion`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_03/Solution.lean#L15) extracts a single $N$ from that eventual statement. This is also a useful reading route: begin with the public statement and endpoint, inspect the parity assembly and symmetric limit, then follow the core, moment, and envelope estimates as needed. Supporting declarations use the namespace `Kourovka213`.

## Reading and verification

The counting here is symbolic mathematics proved in Lean, including finite-set identities, support estimates, and analytic limiting arguments. No external GAP or Magma output, finite search certificate, or unproved classification statement is a hypothesis of the accepted endpoints. The [verification record](../nilradical-v0-verification/README.md) documents fresh project compilation, comparison with independently reviewed statements, and proof replay by Lean and Nanoda under the three-axiom policy. The [statement audit](../nilradical-v0-verification/statement-audits/21.3.md) and subsequent human decision concern correspondence with the intended question; they have a different role from kernel checking and do not referee this exposition.

For an ordinary reproduction, use the repository's pinned setup and run `lake build Kourovka.Problems.P21_03.Solution`; the verification record gives the stronger integrity procedure. All source links above identify accepted revision `5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5`. Extracting an effective cutoff or establishing the proposed threshold 21 would require further mathematics and verification. The present account and theorem make no such claim.
